back: C ≈ 6 × N × D FLOPs: 2N per token forward, 4N backward, ignoring the attention term.
Grow parameters and tokens equally: about 20 tokens per parameter (70B model → 1.4T tokens).
Serving cost scales with parameters. A smaller model on more tokens costs more to train once but less to serve forever.

front: GPU-days for 70B on 1.4T tokens (1,000 TFLOP/s peak, 40% MFU)?
back: 5.88 × 10²³ ÷ 4 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 1.47 × 10⁹ GPU-seconds ≈ 17,000 GPU-days; about 8.3 days on 2,048 GPUs.
Observed tokens/s × model FLOPs per token ÷ hardware peak FLOP/s. Counts only useful model maths (PaLM paper).
HFU also counts recomputed work such as activation recomputation, so HFU ≥ MFU. PaLM 540B: 46.2% MFU, 57.8% HFU.
About per-component MTBF ÷ N. 50,000 h per GPU over 16,384 GPUs ≈ 3 hours.
466 interruptions: 47 planned, 419 unexpected, about 78% of the unexpected attributed to confirmed or suspected hardware issues.
Hardware producing wrong results with no error raised. Detected, if at all, by anomalies such as loss or gradient-norm spikes.
Restart from a checkpoint about 100 steps before the spike and skip roughly 200–500 data batches.
τ ≈ √(2δM): δ = blocking checkpoint time, M = job MTBF. Waste ≈ δ/τ + τ/(2M) + R/M.

front: What goes in a training checkpoint?
back: Weights, optimiser state, LR schedule position, RNG states and the data loader position. About 14 bytes per parameter with Adam.

front: Why do stragglers matter more at scale?
back: Step time is the max over ranks. With 0.1% slow chance per GPU per step, 16,384 GPUs almost always include a slow one.

front: Hard part of the training data pipeline?
back: Not bandwidth (megabytes a second) but deterministic resume, mixture control, dedup and benchmark decontamination.
SFT on demonstrations, a reward model trained on human comparisons, then PPO against the reward with a penalty for drifting from the start model.
Training: one GPU stops the whole gang-scheduled job. Inference: one replica fails only its in-flight requests.
